Abstract
Machine learning (ML) and deep learning methods have demonstrated exceptional performance in diverse domains, including
computer vision, speech and face recognition, autonomous vehicles, the Internet of Things, and cybersecurity. Despite these
advances, the vulnerability of ML systems to adversarial attacks, which introduce perturbations to fool classiﬁers and detectors,
poses signiﬁcant security challenges. As the artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) industry increasingly adopts edge computing, the
security of AI models becomes critical. Edge devices, constrained by limited computational resources, must run smaller
models to achieve comparable latency to cloud-based models on more powerful servers. This work evaluates the impact of
adversarial attacks-malicious perturbations designed to degrade the accuracy and reliability of ML models-on recent YOLO
detectors from the widely used Ultralytics framework. Speciﬁcally, we focus on adversarial patches-carefully crafted patterns
overlaid on an image to mislead object detectors into ignoring or misclassifying objects. We create effective naturalistic
adversarial patches for recent versions of the Ultralytics YOLO models (YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLOv9, and YOLOv10)
by upgrading an existing state-of-the-art patch generation approach designed for an earlier YOLOv4 model. We evaluate
the attacks on the INRIA and on the MPII datasets across multiple YOLO models. The experimental results demonstrate
high effectiveness in object detection evasion in recent models. The results suggest that larger models are more robust to
adversarial attacks than their smaller counterparts. We run inference experiments on edge AI devices to highlight the response
time improvement achieved by using smaller models, albeit at a higher risk of attack.

domains such as computer vision, speech and facial recog-
nition, autopilot and autonomous vehicles, the Internet of
Things, and cybersecurity. Notwithstanding, the systems

either during training or testing, raising signiﬁcant concerns.
Adversarial machine learning (AML) focuses on the study of
a category of attacks designed to degrade the accuracy and
reliability of classiﬁers in performing their assigned tasks.
Common adversarial attacks are categorised as evasion
[1], which alters inputs during the testing phase to produce
incorrect outputs; poisoning [2], which corrupts training data
to compromise model integrity; inversion [3], which uses
model predictions to extract the training data; and model
extraction [4], which uses a query access to the target model
to obtain a new model whose performance is equivalent to
the target model. These attacks often exploit the inherent vul-
nerabilities in ML and DL models by introducing carefully
crafted perturbations that remain imperceptible to humans
yet signiﬁcantly impact model predictions. Speciﬁcally,
adversarial examples-also referred to as adversarial patches

in some contexts-are small, intentional modiﬁcations applied
to input data, causing the model to misclassify them with high
conﬁdence. Such perturbations can be generated through
techniques like the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)
[5], Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) [6], Carlini & Wag-
ner (C&W) [7], Localised and Visible Adversarial Noise
(LaVAN)[8],andOne-Pixel[9].FGSM,PGD,andC&Wpri-
oritise imperceptibility and optimization efﬁciency in digital
domains, typically requiring full access to model gradients
and the input at inference time. While highly effective in
controlled, white-box settings, such methods are constrained
by their dependence on real-time, per-image perturbation
computation, limiting their applicability in scenarios where
adversarial inputs must be precomputed, reused, or deployed
in the physical world. The LaVAN attack introduces localised
adversarial noise conﬁned to a small image region, targeting
object detectors without altering the entire image; however,
it lacks naturalism and often produces conspicuous artifacts.
Nonetheless, naturalistic adversarial patches, such as those
explored in this work, emphasise practicality, realism, and
cross-model transferability.
Traditional cloud computing, where large AI models typ-
ically run, faces signiﬁcant challenges, such as high latency,
bandwidth consumption, and potential privacy issues.
Although large models have greater knowledge capacity than
small models, they can be computationally expensive to
evaluate, typically scaling quadratically with the number of
parameters. Small models are typically generated by model
distillation, the process of transferring knowledge from a
large model to a smaller one. Small models offer several key
advantages: i) Efﬁciency: they use fewer parameters, mak-
ing them more cost-effective to operate; ii) Flexibility: their
simplicity makes them easier to replicate; iii) Reliability:
faster deployment times and the ability to run more replicas
at the same cost improve system reliability; iv) Inference on
CPU: if small enough, these models can perform inference
using CPU SIMD instructions (e.g, AVX-512, Neon/SVE),
which is signiﬁcantly cheaper than using accelerators; v)
Predictability: lower inference latency and reduced tail dis-
tribution make system performance more predictable; vi)
Throughput: the ability to run more replicas increases par-
allelism and overall throughput; and vii) on-device: smaller
models are easier to port for on-device inference, which is not
only a growing trend but also necessary for speciﬁc use cases
such as personal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
and autonomous agents.
With the rapid growth of data and the Internet of Every-
thing, edge computing, which processes data closer to its
source, offers a promising solution by relieving the burden
on data centres and reducing latency [10]. Many companies,
such as large cloud providers, telcos or regional data centre
providers, are starting to offer edge resources as a service
(including compute, storage and networking) close to end
users [11]. As the AI industry embraces the edge as part of
its infrastructure, the security of AI models is a critical issue.
Edge devices must run smaller models with fewer resources
to achieve the same latency as cloud-based models running
on more powerful servers, making the former more vulnera-
ble to adversarial attacks.
In this work, we aim to generate and evaluate the effec-
tiveness of adversarial patches for both large and small object
detection models that have not previously been subjected to
such attacks, or that achieve a level of success not previously
documented. Previous research has demonstrated various
methods for creating adversarial patches against object
recognition models, including misleading attention and clas-
siﬁcation techniques [12], trust region-based optimisation
approaches [13], and generative adversarial network-based
attacks under complex conditions [14]. However, these meth-
ods either focus ondifferent attackstrategies or target speciﬁc
object detection models. In contrast, our approach builds
on and extends the work of [15], which trained adversar-
ial patches for YOLOv4, by adapting it for compatibility
with the widely used Ultralytics framework1. This adaptation
includes modifying the framework to support backpropaga-
tion of gradients for adversarial patches, allowing researchers
to train adversarial patches for object recognition models
using diverse optimisation techniques.
The main contributions of this work can be summarised
as follows:
– We created effective naturalistic adversarial patches, i.e.
patches that resemble real objects, for recent versions
of the Ultralytics YOLO models (YOLOv5, YOLOv8,
YOLOv9 and YOLOv10) by upgrading and customizing
an existing patch generation approach designed for an
older YOLOv4 model.
– We tailored the Ultralytics framework to enable the use
of YOLO models as detectors in the training phase of
naturalistic adversarial patch generation.
– We conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the
effectiveness of the naturalistic adversarial patches, gen-
erated using different Ultralytics YOLO models in the
training phase, across multiple YOLO models. The trans-
ferability of adversarial patches, deﬁned as their ability
to effectively deceive models other than the one used for
their generation, was also evaluated.
– We performed model inference experiments on edge AI
devices with the naturalistic patches generated in this
work, highlighting the importance of research in adver-
sarial machine learning for developing robust and secure
models that balance security and performance, especially
for edge devices.

2 Related work
Thorough reviews of work on the adversarial security of
machine learning, pattern recognition, and deep neural net-
works have been developed in recent years. In [16], a threat
model framework for evaluating the security of machine
learning algorithms is outlined, detailing the attacker’s goals,
knowledge, and capabilities. Defence strategies were cat-
egorised into reactive and proactive approaches. Reactive
defences, such as adversarial training and data sanitisation,
respond to identiﬁed threats, while proactive defences, such
as robust model design and defensive distillation, aim to
anticipate and mitigate potential attacks before deployment.
In [17], the mechanisms by which adversarial attacks are exe-
cuted during both the training and testing phases is explored,
and emphasised the importance of developing more robust
models capable of withstanding adversarial manipulation.
They also emphasised efﬁcient privacy protection methods,
such as differential privacy and homomorphic encryption, to
protect sensitive data and model parameters.
In the cybersecurity domain, [18] examines the impact
of AML, with a particular focus on on intrusion detec-
tion systems (IDS) and malware detection scenarios. The
use of generative adversarial networks (GANs) and genetic
algorithms to generate adversarial malware examples were
identiﬁed. Despite the focus on attack strategies, defence
mechanisms such as adversarial training, gradient mask-
ing, defensive distillation, and feature squeezing were also
discussed. In [19], an in-depth examination of the security
challenges and the signiﬁcant security risks faced by con-
nected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) is provided, which
rely heavily on ML and DL, due to AML. These vehicles
are also vulnerable to attacks from the physical world, where
adversarial examples may include altering trafﬁc signs and
generating adversarial perturbations that evade detection by
state-of-the-art object detection models such as YOLO and
Mask R-CNN. AML is surveyed in [20] with a focus on
defending against adversarial attacks in image classiﬁcation.
DL algorithms, in particular convolutional neural networks
(CNNs), have achieved state-of-the-art performance in var-
ious image classiﬁcation tasks and are increasingly used
in safety-critical applications such as biometric recognition
systems and medical devices. These algorithms are vulner-
able to adversarial examples, such as images with subtle
perturbations, which can fool classiﬁers into making incor-
rect predictions with high conﬁdence. The attacks have
been categorised based on perturbation scope, visibility, and
measurement, highlighting the different types of adversar-
ial images such as individual-scoped and universal-scoped
perturbations.
Morerecently,acomprehensivereviewofexistingdefence
mechanisms against adversarial attacks has been conducted
[21]. This review categorizes defence strategies into mitiga-
tion and detection methods, and evaluates their effectiveness
in domains such as audio, cybersecurity, natural language
processing (NLP), and computer vision. On the one hand,
mitigation strategies, including adversarial training, defen-
sive distillation, ensemble methods, and preprocessing tech-
niques, aim to improve the robustness of ML models by
incorporating adversarial examples during training, trans-
ferring knowledge from robust models, and transforming
input features. Adversarial training, widely used in com-
puter vision and explored in other domains, involves training
models with adversarial examples to improve robustness.
Defensive distillation and ensemble methods improve model
robustness by exploiting knowledge transfer and combining
multiple models, respectively. On the other hand, detec-
tion strategies focus on identifying and rejecting adversarial
examples through supervised and semi-supervised learning,
distance-based methods, feature squeezing, and statistical
approaches. These strategies enhance the ability of ML mod-
els to detect anomalies and maintain integrity in the presence
of adversarial perturbations.
In the domain of object detection, several works have been
carried out for early versions of YOLO models. A robust
physical adversarial sticker generation method is proposed in
[22], based on an extended Expectation Over Transformation
(EOT) for tiny-YOLO and the experiments were validated on
random images from ImageNet. A serious adversarial vulner-
ability in YOLO detectors is identiﬁed in [23] by evaluating
the impact of adversarial attacks sourced from the multiple
task losses (i.e., objectness, localisation, and classiﬁcation)
and designed an effective attack for YOLOv4. The authors
state that this attack is likely to be applicable to other detec-
tors, but no experiments are provided to support this claim.
The vulnerability of DL-based object detectors to adversarial
attacks is analysed in [24], particularly in complex occlusion
scenarios. A two-stage method based on Generative Adver-
sarial Networks (GANs), called TS-GAN, was proposed.
In the ﬁrst stage, a generator is trained using an occlusion
rule to simulate different occlusion scenarios, while in the
second stage, latent variables are optimised to produce the
most effective adversarial patches. The performance of these
adversarial patches has been evaluated evaluated using the
YOLOv2, YOLOv4tiny and Faster R-CNN object detectors.
Morerecently,naturalisticadversarialpatcheshavebeengen-
erated in [25], resembling potted plants, speciﬁcally designed

3 Methods
3.1 Naturalistic Adversarial Patches
This work focuses on the generation of adversarial patches
that resemble real objects in order to evade the detection of
people on the latest Ultralytics YOLO object detector mod-
els. The adversarial patches are generated by optimizing the
latent space of a pre-trained GAN rather than directly modi-
fying pixel values. This approach leverages the natural image
manifoldlearnedbytheGAN,therebyproducingpatchesthat
appear realistic while fooling the detector.
The generation process begins with a GAN generator G
that is pre-trained on the ImageNet [27] dataset. A latent
vector z ∈Rd is sampled from a standard normal distribution
to produce an initial patch P = G(z) ∈RH×W×3. The patch
is then iteratively reﬁned by updating z via gradient descent
in order to minimize the overall loss function deﬁned as:

The naturalistic adversarial patch generation process
developed in this work is illustrated in Fig. 1. First, objects
in the original image are detected using a preselected object
detection model from the Ultralytics framework. Next, the
naturalistic looking adversarial patch is generated by the
GAN. Then, a transformation process is applied to the orig-
inal image to overlay the adversarial patch centred on the
bounding boxes of the objects detected in the ﬁrst step, yield-
ing the patched image. Finally, the object detection model is
re-run on the patched image to obtain the detection results.
These results are used to compute the detection loss func-
tion, denoted by Ldet. This is followed by the addition of
the total variation loss function Ltv to give the total loss,
Ltotal. The total loss is used to update the latent vector, z,
of the GAN. This process is repeated until the adversar-
ial patch is generated. The stopping criterion used in the
patch generation to ensure that the model has learned effec-
tively without overﬁtting or underﬁtting is a ﬁxed number of
epochs. ReduceLROnPlateau with a patience of 50 epochs is
employed in all experiments. Early stopping is not used, so
training is always conducted for the predetermined number
of epochs regardless of the learning rate.

4 Experimental results
We have conducted an experimental design to evaluate the
effectiveness of adversarial patches across the latest YOLO
models generated using the approach described above. The
results of these experiments are presented in this section.
4.1 Hardware platforms
The experiments conducted in this work were performed on
three hardware platforms, as shown in Table 2. Both the
server and workstation platforms were used for both adver-
sarial patch generation and person detection through model
inference, while the edge AI device was used exclusively
for model inference. To run the experiments on these sys-
tems, several cross-platform Docker containers were crafted
to ensure the reproducibility of the results and ease of deploy-
ment across different environments.

4.2 Implementation details
In order to use the Ultralytics framework as a detector in
the optimisation phase of patch generation, both the frame-
work and the adversarial patch generation method have
been upgraded. The modiﬁcations to both software pack-
ages are available via public GitHub repositories.2,3 Firstly,
it was necessary to implement the training, evaluation, and
loss function calculation processes. Second, the gradients of
the predictions of the YOLO models had to be propagated
through the loss functions to update the adversarial patches.
4.3 Evaluation
The adversarial patches generated in these experiments
were initially evaluated using the INRIA Person dataset.
Subsequently, the most effective patches and method con-
ﬁgurations were assessed on the MPII Human Pose dataset

attacks. Together, these evaluations also served to assess the
implications for edge AI security.

5 Discussion
In the above experiments, we have shown that different nat-
uralistic adversarial patches can be generated to effectively
evade the detection of pedestrians in images by the latest
Ultralytics YOLO models. The four most effective patches
on a scale of 0.20, denoted as patch17, patch26, patch27
and patch38, showed an average mAP of 55.72%, 55.09%,
51.43% and 51.47%, respectively, across all models eval-
uated on the INRIA person dataset. In comparison to the
baseline presented in Table 4, the experiment designated as
patch27 showed a 52.22% improvement over the random
baseline for the YOLOv10s model, and the patch patch38,
showed a 51.92% improvement for the YOLOv10n model.
The improvement achieved in mAP by these four adversarial

The results highlight the generalizability and robustness of
the adversarial patches across different datasets. While base-
line patches (white, grey, random) and prior methods such
as Faster R-CNN and advyolo showed moderate effective-
ness, the patches generated in this work consistently achieved
lower mAP values, indicating stronger attack performance.
Notably, the performance degradation was even more pro-
nounced on the MPII dataset, as shown in Table 10, where
several patches reduced mAP below 20% for certain models.

The performance of these patches is signiﬁcantly better
than the baseline patches, demonstrating that the natural-
istic adversarial patch generation method, when combined
with the Ultralytics framework during training, is effective
in generating patches capable of fooling the latest YOLO
object detectors. It is also notable that the effectiveness of the
naturalistic adversarial patches in YOLOv8 and YOLOv9 is
less signiﬁcant compared to earlier models such as YOLOv5.
This observation may indicate that newer models are more
robust to adversarial attacks. However, the same adversarial
patches are more effective at evading YOLOv10, as shown
in Table 7, indicating that newer models do not consistently
show increase robustness to adversarial attacks.
An initial hypothesis for this variability could be related
to the number of parameters in each model. Newer models
tend to be more sophisticated and often require fewer param-
eters. For example, YOLOv8m has 25.9 million parameters,
while YOLOv9m and YOLOv10m have 20.0 million and
15.4 million parameters, respectively. However, this hypoth-
esis is challenged by a counterexample involving YOLOv9s
and YOLOv10s, where YOLOv9s uses 7.1 million param-
eters and YOLOv10s uses 7.2 million, yet the adversarial
attack is more effective on YOLOv10s than on YOLOv9s.
This suggests that factors related to the model architecture
may contribute to the susceptibility to adversarial attacks. For
example, the YOLOv9 model architecture is based on vision
transformers, while YOLOv10 is based on a more reﬁned
and complex model with multiple sequential convolutional
layers [32].

6 Conclusion
In this work we have successfully adapted the Ultralytics
framework to enable its models to be used as detectors in the
training phase of naturalistic adversarial patches in a state-
of-the-art method. Adaptations such as the one implemented
in this work can be developed for other patch generation
methods, making the creation of adversarial patches for new
object detectors more affordable and efﬁcient. The source
code developed in this work is freely available via public
repositories for further research and evaluation.
We have also evaluated the effectiveness of naturalis-
tic adversarial patches on the latest versions of Ultralytics
YOLO object detectors. The experiments performed in this
work were successful in creating adversarial patches for the
YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLOv9 and YOLOv10 models using
123

YOLOv5, YOLOv8 and YOLOv9 as detectors in the training
phase. To the best of our knowledge, these experiments rep-
resent one of the ﬁrst documented attacks on a YOLOv8
model and the ﬁrst documented attacks on YOLOv9 and
YOLOv10 models based on naturalistic adversarial patches.
These results highlight the potential vulnerabilities of current
YOLO models, particularly small models designed to run on
edge AI devices, which aim to achieve the same latency as
cloud-based models running on more powerful servers.
While this work has focused on evaluating the vulnera-
bility of YOLO detectors to naturalistic adversarial patches,
future work should investigate effective defence mechanisms
tailored to this class of attacks. One promising direction is
adversarial training using patch-augmented datasets, where
models are exposed to adversarial patches during training
to increase their robustness. However, this approach is com-
putationally intensive and may reduce generalisation if not
carefully balanced. Detection-based defences, which aim to
identify adversarial artefacts prior to inference, using sta-
tistical anomalies, saliency analysis, or frequency domain
patterns, could be extended to speciﬁcally target localised
and naturalistic patches. In parallel, model-level defences,
such as robust feature extraction architectures or atten-
tion mechanisms that down-weight spurious regions, may
provide improved resilience to spatially constrained pertur-
bations. Furthermore, given the increasing importance of
edge AI, future research should also explore lightweight,
resource-efﬁcient defences that operate within the hard-
ware limitations of edge devices while maintaining detection
latency and accuracy. In addition, a combination of multi-
layered defences, from data to architecture to deployment,
may be required to mitigate the evolving threat landscape
posed by naturalistic adversarial patches.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) and deep learning methods have demonstrated exceptional performance in diverse domains, including computer vision, speech and face recognition, autonomous vehicles, the Internet of Things, and cybersecurity. Despite these advances, the vulnerability of ML systems to adversarial attacks, which introduce perturbations to fool classiﬁers and detectors, poses signiﬁcant security challenges. As the artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) industry increasingly adopts edge computing, the security of AI models becomes critical. Edge devices, constrained by limited computational resources, must run smaller models to achieve comparable latency to cloud-based models on more powerful servers. This work evaluates the impact of adversarial attacks-malicious perturbations designed to degrade the accuracy and reliability of ML models-on recent YOLO detectors from the widely used Ultralytics framework. Speciﬁcally, we focus on adversarial patches-carefully crafted patterns overlaid on an image to mislead object detectors into ignoring or misclassifying objects. We create effective naturalistic adversarial patches for recent versions of the Ultralytics YOLO models (YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLOv9, and YOLOv10) by upgrading an existing state-of-the-art patch generation approach designed for an earlier YOLOv4 model. We evaluate the attacks on the INRIA and on the MPII datasets across multiple YOLO models. The experimental results demonstrate high effectiveness in object detection evasion in recent models. The results suggest that larger models are more robust to adversarial attacks than their smaller counterparts. We run inference experiments on edge AI devices to highlight the response time improvement achieved by using smaller models, albeit at a higher risk of attack.
